title: Fast constant-factor fully dynamic edit distance
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(A\ge1\) and a randomized fully dynamic data structure that maintains two strings of length at most \(N\), after polynomial preprocessing and in polynomial space, under arbitrary single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions, with expected amortized update time \((\log(2+N))^{O(1)}\) and constant query time, returning \(D\) with \(\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\le D\le A\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) at each specified query against an oblivious update sequence?
definitions:
Fix a maximum length \(N\ge2\) and alphabet \(\Sigma=[N]\), with symbols occupying \(O(\log N)\) bits. Both strings may be empty. An update identifies one string and a current position, then inserts one symbol into a gap, deletes one existing symbol, or replaces one symbol. Only valid updates keeping both lengths at most \(N\) are required. Edit distance is the minimum number of unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming one entire string into the other.

Use a word RAM with word size \(\Theta(\log N)\), large enough to address the allowed polynomial storage. Word arithmetic, comparisons, bit operations and a random-access read or write cost one. The data structure has a uniform finite program. For some absolute exponent \(c\), preprocessing and storage are at most \(N^c\). For every fixed finite legal sequence of \(t\) updates, the expected total update cost, excluding preprocessing, is at most \(C t(\log(2+N))^c\). Expectation is over the data structure's internal randomness.

The entire sequence of updates and query times is chosen independently of that randomness and of answers; this is the oblivious-adversary convention. At each fixed query time, the approximation inequalities hold with probability at least \(2/3\). The statement does not require one probability event covering infinitely many queries or robustness to answer-dependent updates. The returned value is a numerical estimate only, not an alignment or edit script. Multiplicative approximation forces \(D=0\) when the strings agree.

The factor \(A\) is independent of maximum length, alphabet and the update history. Neither an \(N^{o(1)}\) factor nor \(N^{o(1)}\) update time implies the requested constant and polylogarithmic bounds. The alphabet and error/adversary conventions above make the imported editorial strengthening explicit.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction and proof of all stated space, initialization, update, query and approximation guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation in this model. Bounds for substitutions only, small-distance promises, static strings, or subpolynomial rather than polylogarithmic update time are insufficient. Conditional impossibility results must retain their assumptions.
context:
Kociumaka, Mukherjee and Saha give a fully dynamic algorithm allowing edits at arbitrary positions in either string. Their main guarantee combines subpolynomial approximation with subpolynomial amortized expected update time.

The constant-factor and polylogarithmic combination is an editorial strengthening of that research direction from the catalogue, not a verbatim named conjecture asserted by the paper. The present card explicitly uses an oblivious adversary and per-query success.
why: This would make a fundamental sequence-distance estimate efficiently maintainable throughout an evolving input.

import_provenance.original_title: Fast constant-factor fully dynamic edit distance
import_provenance.original_statement: Maintain a constant-factor approximation to edit distance between two strings under arbitrary single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions, using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time after polynomial preprocessing. The known joint work achieves subpolynomial approximation and update time, leaving this stronger combination open.
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: This is an editorial strengthening of their tradeoff; exact algorithms whose update time depends on the current distance do not provide this guarantee for arbitrary strings.

sentences: Two strings change through insertions, deletions and substitutions at arbitrary positions.
The goal is a constant-factor estimate of their current edit distance after each update.
The selected data structure allows polynomial initialization and requires polylogarithmic expected amortized updates and constant-time queries.
The cited result obtains subpolynomial factors and times, which are weaker guarantees.
The question asks whether general sequence similarity can be maintained at the cost of elementary dynamic operations.
